newsitem.title: USA: New England Electric seeks bids for 18 plants.
newsitem.headline: New England Electric seeks bids for 18 plants.

text.p: New England Electric System, one of New England's largest utilities, is soliciting bids for 18 of its non-nuclear electric generating plants, possibly setting up one of the first asset sales in electricity deregulation, one possible buyer said Thursday.
The plants are valued at $1.1 billion on company books and are located in Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Vermont and Rhode Island. They are rated for 3,962 megawatts of electricity.

New England Electric has small share in the three Millstone nuclear power plants operated by Northeast Utilities are shut down for safety reasons, and if the closure lasts for a long time, their prices could rise.

Westborough, Mass.-based New England Electric has set a March 14 deadline for nonbinding bids, and has said it has not made a commitment to accept any offer, although decisions are expected in June, one of the bidders told Reuters in a telephone interview. Buyers could bid for all or some of the plants. Any sale would have to be approved by state regulators.
The purchasers are considered to be large interstate utilities and insiders said the bidding list will signal which firms have nationwide acquisition strategies.
The Atlanta-based "Southern Co. is evaluating whether they should put in a bid," said Harold T. Judd, the company's national regulatory manager.
A published report identified Duke Power Co., Charlotte, N.C., and CalEnergy, of Omaha, as other possible bidders.
New England Electric declined to comment. The utility has said in the past that it intends to divest itself of all its generating assets and become solely a transmission and distribution utility.

Judd said the plants up for sale include 15 hydroelectric facilities in Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Vermont, some of which have just been relicensed. It also includes the new 495-megawatt Manchester Street Station in Providence, recently modernized to use natural gas as fuel.
In New England, where environmental rules and citizen opposition make it hard to site new power plants, insiders said any existing licensed plant should attract premium prices.

New England Electric has small share in the three Millstone nuclear power plants operated by Northeast Utilities that are shut down for safety reasons, and if the closure lasts for a long time, prices for the non-nuclear plants could rise.

Westborough, Mass.-based New England Electric has set a March 14 deadline for nonbinding bids, and has said it has not made a commitment to accept any offer, although decisions are expected in June, one of the bidders told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Buyers could bid for all or some of the plants. Any sale would have to be approved by state regulators.
